notes.definition: Our model of the atom has changed over time as new experimental evidence was found: from indivisible spheres, to the plum pudding model, to the nuclear model with electrons in shells, protons and neutrons.
explanation: Scientific models change when new experimental evidence cannot be explained by the existing model. Before the electron was discovered, atoms were thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided into anything smaller. The discovery of the electron, a tiny negatively charged particle, showed that atoms do contain smaller particles. This led to the plum pudding model, which suggested that the atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it. The positive charge and the mass were thought to be spread throughout the atom.

The alpha particle scattering experiment tested the plum pudding model. Positively charged alpha particles were fired at a very thin sheet of gold foil. The plum pudding model predicted that they would all pass straight through, or be deflected only very slightly, because the positive charge was spread out. In fact, most alpha particles did pass straight through, but a few were deflected through large angles and a very small number bounced back towards the source.

These results led to the conclusion that the mass of an atom is concentrated at its centre, in a tiny nucleus, and that the nucleus is positively charged. Because most alpha particles passed straight through, most of the atom must be empty space. The rare alpha particles that came very close to a nucleus were repelled by its positive charge, and those that hit it almost head on bounced back. The nuclear model, with a small positive nucleus surrounded by electrons, replaced the plum pudding model.

Niels Bohr adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances. These fixed orbits are the energy levels, or shells, used today. Bohr's theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations, which is why his model was accepted.

Later experiments led to the idea that the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles, each with the same amount of positive charge. These particles were named protons. The experimental work of James Chadwick provided the evidence that neutrons, with no charge, also exist in the nucleus. This was about 20 years after the nucleus had become an accepted scientific idea. The modern model therefore has protons and neutrons in a tiny nucleus, with electrons in shells around it.
keyFacts: Early model: atoms were tiny spheres that could not be divided.
The discovery of the electron led to the plum pudding model.
Plum pudding model: a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.
Alpha scattering: most alpha particles went straight through, a few were deflected, a very few bounced back.
Conclusion: the mass is concentrated in a tiny, positively charged nucleus, and most of the atom is empty space.
The nuclear model replaced the plum pudding model.
Niels Bohr: electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances (shells); his calculations agreed with experiments.
The positive charge of the nucleus is made of protons, each with the same positive charge.
James Chadwick provided evidence for neutrons, about 20 years after the nucleus was accepted.
Models change when new evidence cannot be explained by the existing model.

keyTerms.definition: A simplified description of something that explains observations and can be used to make predictions.
A model of the atom as a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.
A small, positively charged particle used in the scattering experiment to probe atoms.
An experiment in which alpha particles were fired at thin gold foil; the pattern of deflection showed atoms have a small, positive nucleus.
A model of the atom with a tiny, positively charged nucleus containing most of the mass, surrounded by electrons.
The tiny central part of an atom, containing protons and neutrons and almost all of the mass.
A specific distance from the nucleus at which electrons orbit, as suggested by Niels Bohr.

workedExamples.title: Linking evidence to conclusions
workedExamples.question: In the alpha scattering experiment, a very small number of alpha particles bounced back from the gold foil. What does this tell us about the atom?
steps: Alpha particles are positive, so they are repelled by positive charge.
To bounce back, an alpha particle must meet something with a large positive charge and a large mass concentrated in a small space.
Because only a very small number bounced back, this region must be very small compared with the whole atom.
workedExamples.answer: The positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a very small nucleus at the centre of the atom.

workedExamples.title: Comparing predictions with results
workedExamples.question: Explain why the alpha scattering results could not be explained by the plum pudding model.
steps: In the plum pudding model, positive charge and mass are spread evenly through the atom.
Spread-out charge would only cause tiny deflections, so the model predicts that all alpha particles pass straight through or nearly straight through.
The experiment showed some large deflections and a few alpha particles bouncing back, which the model cannot explain.
workedExamples.answer: The plum pudding model predicts no large deflections, but large deflections and bounce-backs were observed, so the model had to be replaced by the nuclear model.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the plum pudding model has a nucleus.
misconceptions.right: In fact the plum pudding model has no nucleus; the positive charge is spread through the whole atom with electrons embedded in it.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that most alpha particles bounced back.
misconceptions.right: In fact most went straight through. Only a very small number bounced back, which is why the nucleus must be tiny.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the neutron was discovered at the same time as the nucleus.
misconceptions.right: In fact James Chadwick provided evidence for neutrons about 20 years after the nucleus became accepted.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think an old model was simply a mistake.
misconceptions.right: In fact each model explained the evidence available at the time; it was replaced only when new evidence could not be explained.

realWorld: Particle accelerators such as those at CERN use the same idea as the scattering experiment: firing particles at targets to find out what is inside them.
The development of the atomic model is a classic example of how peer review and new evidence lead scientists to change accepted theories.
Knowing that atoms have a tiny, dense nucleus underpins nuclear power and medical uses of radiation.
examTips: When describing the plum pudding model, mention both the ball of positive charge and the negative electrons embedded in it.
In alpha scattering questions, link each observation to a conclusion: straight through means mostly empty space; deflected or bounced back means a small, positive, massive nucleus.
You do not need details of Bohr's or Chadwick's experiments, but you must know what each contributed.
For compare questions, make paired points such as: plum pudding has positive charge spread out, whereas the nuclear model has positive charge concentrated in the nucleus.
summary: Atoms were first thought to be indivisible spheres.
The discovery of the electron led to the plum pudding model.
Alpha scattering showed a tiny, positive nucleus containing most of the mass.
The nuclear model replaced the plum pudding model.
Bohr suggested electrons orbit at specific distances (shells).
Protons and then neutrons (Chadwick) were found in the nucleus.
Models change when new evidence cannot be explained.

markScheme: 1 mark: new experimental evidence (from the alpha particle scattering experiment)
1 mark: could not be explained by the plum pudding model (for example some alpha particles bounced back)
questions.explanation: Models are changed when new evidence conflicts with them. The plum pudding model could not explain large deflections.

questions.question: Describe how Niels Bohr adapted the nuclear model of the atom and why his idea was accepted.
markScheme: 1 mark: electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances / in energy levels (shells)
1 mark: his theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations
questions.explanation: Bohr's model kept the nucleus but placed electrons in fixed orbits. Agreement between theory and experiment led to its acceptance.

questions.question: Describe the modern model of the atom, naming the particles and stating where each is found.
markScheme: 1 mark: a tiny nucleus at the centre
1 mark: containing protons and neutrons
1 mark: electrons in shells (energy levels) around the nucleus
questions.explanation: The model combines the nuclear model, Bohr's shells, protons and Chadwick's neutrons.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows the paths of some alpha particles near a gold nucleus.
Explain why a very small number of alpha particles bounced back from the gold foil.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 215" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif"><polyline points="20,25 400,25" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="20" y1="25" x2="400" y2="25" stroke="currentColor"/><polygon points="400,25 392.6,21.9 392.6,28.1" fill="currentColor"/><polyline points="20,96 228,96 250,88 266,72 284,50 296,36" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="284" y1="50" x2="296" y2="36" stroke="currentColor"/><polygon points="296,36 288.8,39.6 293.6,43.6" fill="currentColor"/><polyline points="20,108 242,108 249,112 242,116 20,130" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="242" y1="116" x2="20" y2="130" stroke="currentColor"/><polygon points="20,130 27.5,132.6 27.2,126.4" fill="currentColor"/><polyline points="20,140 220,140 260,146 300,154 400,166" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="300" y1="154" x2="400" y2="166" stroke="currentColor"/><polygon points="400,166 393.1,162 392.3,168.2" fill="currentColor"/><polyline points="20,195 400,195" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="20" y1="195" x2="400" y2="195" stroke="currentColor"/><polygon points="400,195 392.6,191.9 392.6,198.1" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="260" cy="112" r="7" fill="#fca5a5" fill-opacity="0.6" stroke="currentColor"/><line x1="266" y1="106" x2="330" y2="84" stroke="currentColor"/><text x="334" y="88" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">gold nucleus</text><text x="20" y="20" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">alpha particles</text></svg>

markScheme: 1 mark: they approached (almost head on) the small nucleus, which contains concentrated positive charge and mass
1 mark: the positive nucleus repelled the positive alpha particles (like charges repel), turning them back; very few did this because the nucleus is so small
questions.explanation: Only alpha particles that came very close to a nucleus were strongly repelled. The rarity of bounce-backs shows how small the nucleus is.

questions.question: Describe what later experiments showed about the positive charge of the nucleus.
markScheme: 1 mark: the positive charge could be subdivided into smaller particles
1 mark: each with the same amount of positive charge, named protons
questions.explanation: Every nucleus contains a whole number of protons, each with the same charge (+1 relative charge).

questions.question: Suggest why the plum pudding model predicted that all the alpha particles would pass through the gold foil with little or no deflection.
markScheme: 1 mark: the positive charge (and mass) was spread out through the whole atom
1 mark: so the repulsion on an alpha particle at any point would be too weak to deflect it much
questions.explanation: Large deflections need a concentrated charge and mass. Spreading the charge thinly gives only small forces.

Compare the plum pudding model and the nuclear model of the atom.

markScheme: Indicative content: both models contain negative electrons; both models are neutral overall; plum pudding: ball of positive charge with electrons embedded, mass spread out, no nucleus, no empty space; nuclear: tiny positive nucleus at the centre with most of the mass, electrons outside the nucleus (in shells after Bohr), most of the atom is empty space.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear comparison with at least one similarity and two differences, each referring to both models.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple description of one or both models without direct comparison.
questions.explanation: A comparison should use linking words such as whereas or but, and talk about both models in each point.

questions.question: Use the history of the atomic model to explain how scientific models develop over time.
markScheme: Indicative content: models are based on the evidence available at the time; atoms were first thought indivisible; discovery of the electron was new evidence that led to the plum pudding model; alpha scattering results could not be explained by the plum pudding model, so the nuclear model replaced it; Bohr's model was accepted because calculations agreed with observations; later evidence added protons and then neutrons (Chadwick); models are tested by experiments and changed or replaced when new evidence does not fit.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear explanation of how new evidence leads to changed models, supported by at least two specific examples.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): a simple statement that models change, or a list of models without linking to evidence.
questions.explanation: The key idea is that each change was driven by experimental evidence, not opinion.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows the apparatus used in the alpha particle scattering experiment.
Describe the experiment and its results.
Explain how the results led scientists to replace the plum pudding model with the nuclear model.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 470 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif"><rect x="20" y="100" width="60" height="44" fill="#e5e7eb" fill-opacity="0.6" stroke="currentColor"/><rect x="60" y="118" width="20" height="8" fill="#fde68a" fill-opacity="0.6" stroke="currentColor"/><line x1="80" y1="122" x2="214" y2="122" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><polygon points="214,122 206.6,118.9 206.6,125.1" fill="currentColor"/><rect x="216" y="62" width="6" height="120" fill="#fde68a" fill-opacity="0.7" stroke="currentColor"/><path d="M128.4 86.4A100 100 0 1 1 128.4 157.6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="8 5"/><line x1="222" y1="122" x2="312" y2="122" stroke="currentColor"/><polygon points="312,122 304.6,118.9 304.6,125.1" fill="currentColor"/><line x1="222" y1="122" x2="306" y2="96" stroke="currentColor"/><polygon points="306,96 298,95.2 299.9,101.2" fill="currentColor"/><line x1="222" y1="122" x2="262" y2="34" stroke="currentColor"/><polygon points="262,34 256.1,39.4 261.8,42" fill="currentColor"/><line x1="219" y1="120" x2="140" y2="92" stroke="currentColor"/><polygon points="140,92 145.9,97.4 148,91.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="50" y="160" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">alpha source</text><text x="50" y="174" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">in lead box</text><line x1="222" y1="66" x2="330" y2="22" stroke="currentColor"/><text x="333" y="26" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">thin gold foil</text><line x1="312" y1="190" x2="350" y2="220" stroke="currentColor"/><text x="353" y="224" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">detector</text><text x="148" y="142" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">beam of alpha particles</text></svg>

markScheme: Indicative content: positively charged alpha particles were fired at a very thin gold foil; detectors recorded where they went; the plum pudding model predicted they would all pass through with little or no deflection because positive charge was spread out; results: most passed straight through, so most of the atom is empty space; some were deflected through large angles, so there is a concentrated positive charge that repels them; a very few bounced back, so the mass and positive charge are concentrated in a very small nucleus; because the results could not be explained by the plum pudding model, the nuclear model was proposed: a tiny, positive, massive nucleus with electrons around it.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): describes the method and all three observations, links each to a correct conclusion, and explains why the plum pudding model could not account for the results.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes at least two observations with linked conclusions, with some reference to the change of model.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple description of the experiment or of one result, with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Top answers pair every observation with a conclusion and contrast the results with what the plum pudding model predicted.

questions.question: Describe how the scientific model of the atom developed from the idea of indivisible spheres to the model that includes neutrons. For each change, explain what new evidence or idea caused it.
markScheme: Indicative content: atoms were first thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided; the discovery of the electron showed atoms contain smaller particles, leading to the plum pudding model (ball of positive charge with electrons embedded); the alpha scattering experiment showed most of the atom is empty space and that mass and positive charge are concentrated in a small nucleus, so the nuclear model replaced plum pudding; Niels Bohr suggested electrons orbit at specific distances, and his calculations agreed with experimental observations; later experiments showed the nuclear charge is made of smaller particles each with the same positive charge (protons); James Chadwick provided evidence for neutrons in the nucleus, about 20 years after the nucleus was accepted.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): describes all main stages in the correct order, each linked to the evidence or idea that caused the change.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes most stages in order with some links to evidence.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): names one or two models or discoveries with little sequence or explanation.
questions.explanation: The sequence is: indivisible spheres, plum pudding (electron), nuclear model (alpha scattering), Bohr's shells (calculations matched experiments), protons, neutrons (Chadwick).
